title: The Fishman home: a community gathering place in David-Horodok
summary: A family home serving as a community center and guesthouse reveals the everyday hospitality that supported communal life.
editorialContent:
## A house beside the river and bridge

In the memorial book’s account, the Fishman home was not simply a family residence. Tzivia and Bracha Fishman remember their parents, [Sarah and Zelman Fishman](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_d3f9c7b7b032e4d4e64c4338), and the [Fishman family home](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_871195c2e34783c6df119504) as a large, elongated house beside the river and bridge. Its many rooms made it possible to welcome guests and host organised activity. The sisters describe it as a meeting place, a library, a headquarters, a guesthouse—and, in their words, “the center of life in the town.” ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html?utm_source=openai))

Those recollections come from the memorial book, in JewishGen’s translation, in a passage identified with the family name פישמן. They preserve the sisters’ testimony, not an independent inventory of the house or its visitors. The account gives no address, dates for the gatherings, or list of travelers who stayed there. It does, however, make clear that the household’s hospitality and political-organisational role were intertwined: people came not only as guests, but to meet, read, plan, and take part in community life.

The sisters say they were one of nine children—four boys and five girls—and that only two sisters survived the “great murder.” Their statement is a family memory of catastrophe as well as of everyday life. It tells us why a home could loom so large in recollection: it held the rhythms of a household, but also offered a place where a much wider circle could gather. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html?utm_source=openai))

## A library, a club, and overlapping movements

According to the sisters, their parents’ home housed the town’s first meeting place and library for the [General Zionist youth club and library](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_b144402db27db970db94b938). It also served as headquarters for the local Mizrachi organisation, a religious Zionist movement. The memoir does not describe the club’s schedule, the library’s collection, or how the different groups shared rooms. But the picture it offers is suggestive: a private home provided practical infrastructure for public-minded activity where a formal organisation needed a place to meet.

The wider memorial book portrays David-Horodok as a town with a lively associational life. Its accounts describe libraries, schools, political groups, youth movements, and self-education circles. One chapter says that a Zionist organisation founded a library in 1917; another describes the growth of libraries after the First World War, including a Poalei Zion library founded in 1925 and a Tarbut-school library. These are distinct recollections elsewhere in the same book—not independent confirmation of the Fishman sisters’ account—but they place the household within a remembered culture in which reading, discussion, and organising were part of communal life. ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Davyd-Haradok/dav036.html?utm_source=openai))

The Fishman home’s role may therefore have been both specific and representative. Specific, because the sisters name their parents’ house and the organisations that used it. Representative, because their story shows how community activity could depend on accessible domestic spaces as well as on institutions with dedicated premises. A library or club did not need to begin in a purpose-built building: it could take shape in rooms made available by a family.

## Hospitality as community infrastructure

The memorial book says that the home “became a house for tending to guests.” It does not identify those guests or explain where they came from. We should not turn that phrase into a roster of refugees or claim that the house served a particular relief programme. What the sisters do establish is a household practice of hospitality alongside its political and cultural functions. Their home could receive people passing through town and host local activity under one roof. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html?utm_source=openai))

That combination points to the importance of informal networks. A traveler needed somewhere to stay; a youth group needed a room; a library needed space and people willing to care for it. In this account, these needs converged in a family home. The Fishmans’ standing in the community may have rested partly on this openness, although the memoir does not explain how the household made decisions about whom to host or how its work was supported. The absence of those details is a limit of the testimony, not evidence that such arrangements were simple.

The sisters also connect their family’s story to danger and rescue. They recall that their eldest brother Moshe, who lived in Lakhva and earned his livelihood from a river boat, helped save many Jews, though he himself did not survive. Their brief account links the household’s welcome to a wider world of movement along the river and mutual aid across towns. It does not say that the Fishman house itself was a rescue centre; that distinction matters. The book’s testimony concerns the home’s gatherings and hospitality, and separately remembers Moshe’s rescue work by boat. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html?utm_source=openai))

## A neighbouring tragedy in the same passage

The printed-page sequence also places the Fishman sisters’ memories near an account of Rabbi Asher Berman, [remembered as a rescuer](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_afe8ff40fb42b73b42030bea). The memorial book recounts that he disappeared while traveling on an errand involving the procurement of meat for the Polish army, and that his body was later found near the [town cemetery](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_07b235283312b895507be083). The passage is associated with [Gershon Barm](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_3c9fd679bfc9ac0f000d2eba), while the preceding account is attributed to [Chaim Kluzhny](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_c1086a410fc7ef70a6202775). ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav092.html?utm_source=openai))

This adjoining story is not testimony about the Fishman household, and it should not be made into one. Its placement does, however, remind readers that the book gathers memories of communal service and peril side by side. Berman’s story concerns the dangers of travel and public responsibility; the Fishman sisters’ account remembers a home that welcomed guests and enabled collective life. Together, they show how the memorial book preserves different kinds of connection—some made in a house, others on the roads between towns.

## What the record can—and cannot—tell us

The Fishman home survives in the record through the sisters’ retrospective account. The book gives us the family’s names, the house’s riverside location, its substantial size, and its uses as a meeting place, library, organisational headquarters, and guesthouse. It does not establish the exact years of these activities or name the visitors and participants. Nor did the independent archival search locate a separate source confirming the house’s role or identifying its guests. A Yad Vashem victims’ list includes David-Horodok as a place of residence for some children, but that broad archival context does not corroborate the Fishman family’s account. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/pdf-drupal/en/download/remembrance/English5000b.pdf?utm_source=openai))

That gap is worth preserving. The home’s significance does not depend on embellishing the testimony. The sisters’ recollection already describes a household whose rooms connected family life to youth politics, religious Zionist activity, reading, and hospitality. In the destroyed community they remembered, the Fishman house mattered because it made those connections possible—and because, for a time, a family opened its doors to the town.
